profile.campus: Widows Creek, Jackson County, Alabama (former TVA Widows Creek Fossil Plant site near Bridgeport)
profile.address: County Road 459, Widows Creek Station, Jackson County, Alabama, 35740
profile.reading: This building sits on the 360-acre former Widows Creek Fossil Plant site near Bridgeport, a coal-fired power plant the Tennessee Valley Authority operated for 63 years, employing more than 500 workers directly, before shutting it down in 2015 as part of TVA's broader coal retirement program. Google announced in April 2018 it would build a roughly $600 million data center on the site, its eighth US data center and fourteenth globally at the time, with TVA committing to supply the facility with renewable power sourced from solar, wind, or hydroelectric generation to meet Google's sustainability goals rather than the coal power the site had produced for decades. Alabama and Jackson County officials framed the project as turning the economic loss of the coal plant's closure into new opportunity, and Google contributed a $100,000 grant to Jackson County schools for STEM programming around the time of the announcement; the fully built-out complex was projected to support 75 to 100 permanent jobs. Google has continued investing in the site well beyond the original announcement: in 2026 the company said it would put in an additional $1.5 billion to expand the campus through 2027, and agreed to cover the electricity its own operations consume plus infrastructure costs tied directly to the facility, a commitment TVA highlighted when it approved a 10% data center electricity rate increase phased in starting October 2026 to keep expansion costs from falling on other ratepayers. Google is also working with TVA and Kairos Power on a next-generation power source for the site: TVA plans to purchase electricity from Kairos' Hermes 2 advanced nuclear demonstration project, with up to 50 megawatts earmarked to support Google's Alabama and Tennessee data centers once that project comes online. Google's data center locations page does not publish which of the two mapped Widows Creek buildings serves which function, nor their individual square footage or MW capacity, so this registry records the campus-level investment and power figures as regional context.

profile.campus: Lithia Springs, Douglas County, Georgia (Google's original Atlanta-metro data center campus, present since 2003)
profile.address: Switch Way, Mableton, Douglas County, Georgia, 30122
profile.reading: This is Google's original Georgia data center campus in Lithia Springs, Douglas County, in the Atlanta metro, where OpenStreetMap tags date Google's presence to 2003, among the company's earliest self-built US data center sites alongside The Dalles, Oregon. Google's initial building on the site totaled roughly 500,000 square feet, and in 2015 the company announced a $300 million expansion to add a second, adjacent building, with construction beginning that summer and completion targeted for 2016; Google said it already employed more than 350 people at the Douglas County campus at the time of that announcement, with the expansion expected to add at least 25 more data center jobs initially. Local and Georgia state officials provided tax incentives to attract the expansion, consistent with the state's broader push to draw hyperscale data center investment, and Google cited the project alongside a separate Singapore expansion announced the same day as evidence of its accelerating global infrastructure build-out. Google reported that its Georgia operations helped generate $2.76 billion of economic activity for roughly 62,000 Georgia businesses in 2014, a period corresponding to the run-up to the second-building announcement. Google has since made a far larger Georgia commitment through a separate, newer project: in April 2026 the company revealed itself as the developer behind the previously unnamed "Project Pegasus," an $8 billion data center campus retrofitting a 600,000-square-foot industrial building in LaGrange, roughly 70 miles southwest of Atlanta, which Google has described as complementing rather than replacing its original Douglas County operations. Google's data center locations page does not publish current square footage or MW capacity for the Douglas County campus specifically, so this registry records the 500,000-square-foot original building figure and the 2015 expansion investment as the best available operator-adjacent figures rather than current totals.

profile.campus: Google Fiber Atlanta metro network, Fulton County, Georgia (exact facility unconfirmed)
profile.address: Near North Avenue Northeast, Old Fourth Ward, Atlanta, Fulton County, Georgia (approximate; OSM coordinates resolve to an unrelated commercial address, not a confirmed Google facility)
profile.reading: This OpenStreetMap point is labeled "Google Fiber" and tagged telecom=data_center, but the evidence gathered this session indicates it is very unlikely to be a hyperscale Google data center of the kind found elsewhere in this registry. Google Fiber is Google's residential and business gigabit internet service, a separate Alphabet business line from Google Cloud's data center infrastructure, and Google Fiber has operated in the Atlanta metro area since the company named Atlanta a "fiber city" in January 2015. Reporting from Atlanta Magazine documented that between mid-2015 and early 2016, Google installed roughly a dozen small "fiber huts," described as structures about the size of a one-car garage costing $150,000 to $250,000 each, distributed around Atlanta to serve as last-mile distribution points feeding 20,000 to 30,000 homes apiece; one such hut is documented in East Point's Sykes Park. These huts are network distribution infrastructure, not data centers, and typically do not carry their own separate commercial street address, which is consistent with this session's reverse-geocoding of this OSM point's stored coordinates resolving to a Sweetgreen restaurant address on North Avenue Northeast in Atlanta's Old Fourth Ward rather than to any confirmable Google-operated building. Google Fiber's Atlanta rollout was also widely reported as troubled: a Google Fiber contractor ruptured utility lines dozens of times during construction, drawing scrutiny from the Georgia Public Service Commission, and as of Atlanta Magazine's reporting only a single building, a College Park apartment complex, had working residential Google Fiber service years after the initial announcement. Given this evidence, this registry treats this point as most likely representing Google Fiber network infrastructure, such as a fiber hut or point-of-presence, mistagged or approximately located in OpenStreetMap, rather than a verifiable Google Cloud data center facility, and declines to assign it fabricated address, square footage, or capacity figures it cannot support with a real source.

profile.address: West 2nd Street, The Dalles, Wasco County, Oregon, 97058
profile.reading: This building is the second of two data center structures Google has built along West 2nd Street on its original Dalles campus, the site where Google began constructing its first self-operated data center in 2006, marking the start of Google building and operating its own data center infrastructure rather than leasing it from third parties. Google's own data center locations page lists Oregon among its earliest and most significant US data center states, and the company has stated it has invested more than $7 billion in Oregon infrastructure since 2006, spread across the multiple buildings that now make up the Dalles campus. Google began construction of a fourth building at the site in 2015, expanding beyond the original two-building footprint reflected in OpenStreetMap's mapping of this location. Google chose The Dalles for its location along the Columbia River, which provided both hydroelectric power access from Bonneville Power Administration dams and river water Google has used for cooling, a choice that later became the subject of a long-running local dispute. Fortune's longform reporting and Oregon Public Broadcasting have both covered tension between Google and the City of The Dalles over how much of the city's water rights the data center campus consumes for cooling, with some residents quoted describing the company's local reputation shifting over nearly two decades of expansion. The Dalles campus predates Google's newer Taylor Lake data center project nearby, and this registry treats the original West 2nd Street buildings and the Taylor Lake buildings as distinct facilities despite sharing the same Wasco County campus and operator. Google has not disclosed which specific building on West 2nd Street this OSM-mapped structure corresponds to, nor its individual power capacity or floor area, consistent with Google's general practice of reporting investment and jobs figures only at the state or metro level rather than per building. This building belongs to Google's Taylor Lake data center, a distinct, newer campus from the original 2006 West 2nd Street site though both sit within The Dalles, Wasco County. Data Center Dynamics reported Google opened phase one of the Taylor Lake facility in 2018, describing it as a two-story, roughly 164,000-square-foot building representing only the first stage of a larger planned project, built at a reported cost of around $600 million. Local coverage from KTVZ and the Columbia Gorge News described a ribbon-cutting event in March 2018 attended by Google and Wasco County officials, with construction at that phase employing more than 1,000 workers and the completed building expected to support roughly 50 permanent jobs, while a subsequent phase was projected to need an additional 750 temporary construction workers. Google's own data center locations page for Oregon reports the state total, more than $7 billion invested since 2006, covering both the West 2nd Street and Taylor Lake campuses together rather than breaking the figure out per site. Google has not published Taylor Lake's current total square footage following later expansion phases, nor its MW power capacity, consistent with the company's general practice of not disclosing per-building operating details. This registry treats the Taylor Lake buildings as a separate facility cluster from the original West 2nd Street campus given their different names, construction timeline, and reported investment figures, while noting both share the same Wasco County, Oregon jurisdiction and Google as operator.

Wasco County's enterprise zone agreement with Google, renewed as each new building at both the West 2nd Street and Taylor Lake campuses comes online, has abated local property taxes on the investment for set terms in exchange for the jobs and payroll Google commits to; county officials have pointed to that structure, alongside Oregon's lack of a state sales tax, as a material reason Google kept expanding in The Dalles rather than concentrating solely in newer data center markets.

profile.campus: Clarksville-Montgomery County, Tennessee (Google's Boolean Drive / Jim Johnson Road campus)
profile.address: Boolean Drive, Montgomery County, Middle Tennessee, Tennessee
profile.reading: This building, tagged SPC1A in OpenStreetMap, was the first phase of Google's Clarksville-Montgomery County data center campus, the company's first data center in Tennessee. Google, the Tennessee Valley Authority, and Governor Bill Haslam's administration announced the roughly $600 million project through the Tennessee Department of Economic and Community Development, and Google formally opened the facility on November 6, 2019, in a ribbon-cutting ceremony led by then-Governor Bill Lee, following a construction start in February 2018. The campus draws power in part through a 413-megawatt renewable energy purchase agreement Google struck with the Tennessee Valley Authority, sourced from solar farms totaling roughly 1.6 million panels across sites in Tennessee and Alabama, one of the larger corporate renewable power deals TVA has signed. Google has said it gave more than $450,000 to local nonprofits and schools in the Clarksville area in the years following the data center's opening, part of a broader community-investment pattern the company has repeated at other US data center sites. Since construction began in 2018, Google reports investing more than $6 billion in Tennessee overall, a figure that under its updated economic-impact methodology includes data center construction along with server and networking capital expenditure rather than construction costs alone, and the company says it helped generate $11.4 billion of economic activity for Tennessee businesses, nonprofits, and developers in 2025. Google's data center locations page and its economic-impact reporting do not break these totals out per building, so this registry records them as regional context rather than facts specific to the SPC1A building, and treats the Boolean Drive address, drawn from OpenStreetMap's reverse-geocoded coordinates, as the best currently available location detail for this structure pending a county assessor parcel lookup.

This building is part of Google's original Midlothian, Texas data center campus, a 375-acre site in the Railport industrial park that the Dallas Morning News reported as a roughly $600 million project when it broke ground, Google's first data center in Texas and one of four the company was simultaneously building in the US at the time alongside facilities in Alabama, Virginia, and Tennessee. The Midlothian campus opened in 2019, and Google said it expected the completed facility to employ around 40 permanent staff, generating hundreds of construction jobs over the build-out; the city of Midlothian offered Google a 10-year tax abatement covering 100% of personal property taxes and 85% of improvement taxes to help attract the project, and Google contributed a $100,000 grant to Midlothian Independent School District for STEM programs. Google has continued expanding the site well past its original single building: on September 2, 2026, Google announced a $40 billion Texas investment through 2027 that includes a fourth Midlothian building backed by nearly $1 billion in additional spending, part of what the company has described as three AI-focused data center hubs across the state. Google's own Ellis County data center location page confirms the campus but, consistent with the company's general disclosure practice, does not publish individual building addresses, square footage, or MW power capacity; a roughly 86-megawatt figure some third-party data center trackers cite for the Midlothian campus has not been confirmed by Google directly and this registry declines to adopt it as fact. This building is one of at least three Google has built along V V Jones Road on the Midlothian campus.
